summary: BGP communities (RFC 1997) are tags providers attach to routes, for example to mark customer, peer, or geographic origin. This Best Current Practice defines standard outbound communities and their encodings for export to BGP route collectors, because that information helps researchers understand the global routing system.

eli5.summary: Route announcements carry little stickers. This agrees on a common set of stickers so researchers who collect them can learn how the internet's roads connect.

subtitle: A standard set of BGP community tags so route collectors can learn how providers classify the routes they carry.

tldr.problem: Providers tag routes with communities to mark customer, peer and geographic origin, but without a common scheme that information is hard to use for understanding the global routing system.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines standard outbound community values, in the form AS number plus a 16-bit value, for route categories, regions and countries, with encodings for RFC 1997 and extended communities.
tldr.outcome: Providers can convert their internal communities to these values when exporting to a route collector, and IANA keeps registries for them.

today: RFC 4384 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 114). It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on RFC 1997 and RFC 4360.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
BGP communities are tags that service providers attach to routes. They are used to tag customer, peer and geographically originated routes, to control how far a route is redistributed, to let customers set attributes such as LOCAL_PREF, to signal VPNs and to carry link bandwidth.

Large-scale BGP data collection and research showed that the geographic, topological and relationship information carried in these communities is essential for a deeper understanding of the global routing system. This memo defines standard communities for export to BGP route collectors. Using them inside a provider is beyond its scope. Data analysts are encouraged to check with their data sources which peers implement the scheme, because much existing data and many legacy peerings predate it.
sections.eli5: Network owners already stick small notes on the routes they pass along. This memo makes everyone write the same kind of note, so people studying the internet can read them.

sections.title: Route Categories
sections.content:
Tagging is often called coloring, and a route's community value is its color. Two providers are peers when they exchange routes via BGP and their traffic exchange is settlement-free. The categories are:

  • Customer routes: heard from a customer via BGP and propagated to peers and other customers.
  • Peer routes: heard from peers and not propagated to other peers, only to the provider's customers.
  • Internal routes: originated by the provider and passed to its peers and customers.
  • Internal more specific routes: used for circuit load balancing and IGP route reduction, and never exported to any external peer.
  • Special purpose routes: anything else that needs a unique value, such as anycast routes and overlay network routes.
  • Upstream routes: learned from an upstream provider under a transit contract.
  • National routes: sourced from or received within a particular country.
  • Regional routes: routes treated differently by region, because a provider may peer with an AS in one region and sell it transit in another.
sections.eli5: Each route gets a sticker saying where it came from: a customer, a friend network, the provider itself, a bigger provider above, or a particular country or region.

sections.title: RFC 1997 Community Encoding
sections.content:
RFC 1997 communities are BGP Type Code 8 and are 32-bit values. The best current practice is to put the provider's 16-bit AS number in the high-order two octets and the classification of the route in the low-order two octets, written <AS>:<Value>. For example, 0x2A7C029A represents AS 10876 with value 666.

The values 0x0000000 through 0x0000FFFF and 0xFFFF0000 through 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved. A provider is expected to convert its internal community values to the standard ones on output to a route collector. The categories are not mutually exclusive, so several communities can be attached to one route.
sections.eli5: The sticker has two halves: the network's own number, and a code saying what kind of route it is.

sections.title: Values for Data Collection
sections.content:
The low-order 16 bits are a number for the first seven categories: 1 for customer, 2 for peer, 3 for internal, 4 for internal more specific, 5 for special purpose and 6 for upstream. Zero is reserved, and so is the range from 0000000000000111 to 0000011111111111.

Values from 0000100000000000 upward encode national and regional routes as <R><X><CC>. <R> is a 5-bit region identifier, <X> is 1 bit set to 1 for satellite links and 0 otherwise, and <CC> is a 10-bit ISO-3166-2 country code. Values 0100000000000000 and above are reserved for national and regional use.

The worked example is a national route over a terrestrial link in AS 10876 from the Fiji Islands: R is 00010 (Oceania), X is 0 and CC is 242, giving low-order bits 0x10F2. A configuration language might write it as 10876:4338.
sections.eli5: The second half of the sticker is either a short number for a basic kind of route, or a small code that says which part of the world and which country the route is tied to.

sections.title: Extended Communities
sections.content:
The standard values may clash with a provider's existing community assignments. Extended communities (RFC 4360) avoid such clashes. The Extended Communities attribute is a transitive optional BGP attribute with Type Code 16.

For data collection the memo uses the two-octet AS specific extended community, with the AS number in the Global Administrator field and the Local Administrator field free to carry any information. It assigns Sub-Type 0x0008, and the Value is carried in the low-order octets of the Local Administrator field. The two high-order octets are reserved, set to 0x00 when sending and ignored on receipt.

A four-octet AS version also exists, using type 0x02 and sub-type 0x0008, with a four-octet AS number assigned by the IANA in the Global Administrator sub-field.
sections.eli5: If the usual sticker clashes with one a network already uses, there is a bigger sticker with room for a different label, so both can be used.

sections.title: BGP UPDATE Packing
sections.content: Data collection communities can make the attribute set of a route more unique, because each route collects data specific to its path through one or more ASes. That can affect whether several routes can be grouped in one BGP update message, and may increase bandwidth use, router CPU cycles and memory.
sections.eli5: If every route has its own special sticker, they cannot travel together in one bundle as easily, so more work is needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo adds no new security considerations to BGP itself. However, the communities may reveal network structure that was not visible outside the provider's network, so care should be taken when exporting them to route collectors. Routes exported to a collector should also be tagged with the NO_EXPORT community (0xFFFFFF01).

The communities are intended for use on egress to a route collector, so an operator may overwrite internal communities with these values. Operators should make sure their BGP implementation behaves well when an added attribute makes a PDU exceed 4096 octets. Since communities are used to implement policy, an overflow could usurp the intended attribute data or cause indeterminate failures, with unintended policy effects.
sections.eli5: The stickers might tell outsiders how a network is built, so they should be shown only to the collector and not passed further.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned Sub-Type 0x0008 in the First Come First Served extended transitive category of the AS specific extended community type. IANA also created two registries for BGP Data Collection Communities, one for standard and one for extended communities, both initially filled with the values from Section 4.

New values, in particular for <Value> or <R>, need IETF Consensus, usually through the Global Routing Operations Working Group (grow).
sections.eli5: An official list keeps track of which sticker codes mean what, and adding a new one needs the community's agreement.
